utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have appearances for today, starting with Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, to my learned colleagues from the Defence, General Delic, everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Matthias Neuner, Laurie Sartorio, Kyle Wood, Aditya Menon, and our case manager Djurdja Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to our learned colleagues from the Prosecution, to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson representing General Rasim Delic, with legal assistants Lejla Gluhic, Lana Deljkic, Asja Zujo, and our intern Claire Bonnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Mr. Robson, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. In this part of our closing arguments, I will be dealing with the Prosecution's crime base allegations, and I will also conclude with a few words on sentencing. Dealing, first of all, with the crime base allegations. Like the Prosecution, I have split this into three main topics: First of all, the issue of the crimes on the 8th of June; second, the July 1995 crimes; and, third, the September 1995 crimes. I will turn to the first topic, the Bikosi crimes. In its closing brief, at paragraph 195, the Prosecution suggests that Mujahedin from the Poljanice camp were engaged in combat with the 306th Brigade in Maline on the 8th of June, 1993; and on Monday, the Prosecution claimed that the involvement of the Mujahedin was not a random incident. In our closing brief, at paragraphs 204 to 209, we have set out in detail how there is no proof that Mujahedin participated in combat with that unit, either in Maline village or elsewhere that day. In its arguments, the Prosecution submitted that the Chamber should place no reliance on what Saban Alic, a Prosecution witness and a Poljanice Mujahedin member, said, and the reasons for that was because they said he been with the Mujahedin less than one week at the time of combat. Your Honours, you will recall that Mr. Alic stated there were no links with the 306th Brigade and that no prior arrangements were made. He said that they learned they would go into combat on the eve of the action itself. What we say is that even if Mr. Alic was a mere foot soldier, the week that he spent with that small group of Mujahedin would have been sufficient for him to find out whether plans were afoot for the Mujahedin to involve themselves in combat with the ARBiH. More importantly, his evidence tied in with what the other Prosecution witnesses had to say, you will recall, that no other Prosecution witnesses mentioned that there was joint combat with the Bosnian army. And, also, members of the 306th Brigade, Osman Fusko and Sinan Begovic, confirmed that the army did not fight alongside the Mujahedin. In its arguments, the Prosecution suggested that the appropriate witness to refer to was Ali Hamad. However, his evidence made it clear at the time of the 8th of June combat, he was based in Bijelo Bucje; and when he tried to head towards the Bila valley, he could get no further than Travnik. And he explained that it took anything up to ten days after the fighting on the 8th of June for him to meet up with the other Mujahedin, and we can see this from transcript pages 60 and 61 of his testimony on the 7th of September of last year. Thus, that witness was not present in Mehurici or Poljanice when plans were made for combat. And also it can be seen from the part of the transcript that the Prosecution referred to the other day, page 29, that he was speaking generally when he spoke about contacts with the ARBiH, and he was not referring to the 8th of June combat. As we set out in our closing brief, he subsequent testimony made it clear that the Mujahedin were not under ARBiH control. On Monday, the Prosecution also showed you some maps marked by witnesses, and they referred to Exhibit 99 and Exhibit 64; however, those exhibits do not show that the Mujahedin fought together with the ARBiH. Yesterday, my colleague touched upon Exhibit 64, which was Sinan Begovic's map, and that was because that was a document based on hearsay. But even if you were to pay attention to that document, what you would see is that there was about a distance of one kilometre between the ARBiH units and the Mujahedin on the 8th of June. So, this, of course, shows that this did not fight alongside each other. Your Honours, I will turn to the issue of Guca Gora, which cropped up in the Prosecution's arguments. And on Monday, the Prosecution suggested that the events involving Ali Hamad at Guca Gora indicated that the Mujahedin chief accepted Alagic's order not to blow up the church. I don't want to say too much about this because it is set out at our closing brief at paragraph 118, and Ms. Vidovic touched upon this yesterday in her arguments. But I would remind that you that Ali Hamad testified that the Mujahedin threatened to kill Mehmed Alagic at the church, and we can see that at transcript page 120 from his testimony on the 8th of September of last year. Also, Ali Hamad confirmed that the reason that Wahiuddin decided not to damage the church was that he estimated that it was not in the Mujahedin's interest to have a conflict with the Bosniaks, and that was at page 121 that that was said. So, Your Honours, neither of these pieces of evidence point to a relationship of effective control. The Prosecution's most important assertion in its closing brief, concerning the Bikosi killings, is that the Mujahedin responsible for the killings were from the Poljanice camp. It claims that the perpetrators emerged from the camp. However, to the contrary, we have explained in paragraph 228 of our closing brief that the evidence varied as to where the Mujahedin appeared from. What is clear, however, is that no witness ever stated that they emerged from the camp, nor did they ever say that they emerged from the external parameter. The Prosecution claims that Halim Husic confirmed that the Poljanice Mujahedin were the only group in the area; however, he testified quite the opposite. I quote from his testimony: "In that period of time, there were several different groups that were often times mutually conflicting and were stationed and active in different areas." He went on to explain about Guca Gora group. Moreover, he said that on the 10th of June, 1993, he saw men in Guca Gora that he subsequently learned were the Turkish Gerila. As he explained in his testimony, the distance from Guca Gora to Bikosi was only two kilometres, and that was along an asphalt road which linked the settlements together, a very short distance, we would say. I would remind you that one of the most surprising features of the Prosecution's case, as set out in its closing brief, is that it has totally ignored all the evidence showing that there were other Mujahedin groups active in Central Bosnia, and this applies to the time-periods in both 1993 and in 1995. In its arguments, the Prosecution suggested that the other Mujahedin, groups which the Defence referred to in its closing brief at paragraph 230, did not have local Bosniak members. Now, in that paragraph, apart from the Poljanice Mujahedin group, we rely on evidence to show there were three other groups in the area: Abu Hamza's group in Guca Gora, the Zenica Turkish Gerila, and Abu Zubeir's group. First of all, dealing with the Zenica Gerila --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did they also have local Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Certainly, the Zenica Gerila; and if we could bring up Exhibit 179, I will show you why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No. I just wanted an answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If it is possible to bring up Exhibit 179 on the screen, what we will see here is a document that the Trial Chamber has come across many times before, and it is the letter of Hadzihasanovic dated the 13th of June 1993. And in this letter, we can see in the first paragraph, he says: "In the general area of Zenica municipality, since the beginning of the war, there have been volunteers from foreign countries, Arabs and Turks, as well as a group of Bosnians trained by them, the so-called Gerila." Your Honours, it is, therefore, clear from this letter that the Gerila group comprised locals; and, similarly, Halim Husic was asked about this in his testimony. A question was put to him by my learned colleague: "Just one moment please. When you say 'Gerila from Zenica,' are these foreigners or locals?" And his reply to that was: "Turkish Gerila comprising mostly foreigners." So he also confirmed that there were some locals within its ranks. Very importantly, in connection with Mr. Husic's evidence, his evidence showed that those Mujahedin, the Turkish Gerila, were operating in that area on the 10th of June, a very short period after the killings. As to the Abu Hamza group, it is not for the Defence to prove there were locals in that group, and we would note that the Prosecution has not called any evidence to show that it was comprised exclusively of foreigners. As to the suggestion that Abu Zubeir's group was comprised exclusively of foreigners, in its arguments the other day, the Prosecution relied upon the statement of PW-9, who stated that as far as he knew, that group was formed only out of the Arabs. However, if you look at that self-same statement, at paragraph 101, we can see that PW-9 first learned of Abu Hamza and his group at the end of 1994. The Prosecution has called no evidence to show that there were no local Bosniak members in the Abu Zubeir group in June 1993, some one and a half years earlier. Therefore, Your Honours, on the evidence the fact that Mujahedin appeared at a location close to the Poljanice camp cannot lead the Trial Chamber to conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that they were members of the Mujahedin group based there. Clearly, it cannot be excluded that the Mujahedin who carried out the killings were members of one of the other groups in the area or even an ad hoc collection of foreign and local persons involved in a criminal venture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Robson, before you move on, on this subject, obviously, what attracts the Chamber's attention is the pattern that was conducted on the 8th of June, in which apparently you see the two formations moving down. This was, I admit, this was the testimony of this soldier that you mentioned; but, still, we have no reasons to doubt that what he told us about the way they moved that day was true. So it looked as if there was a coordinated movement by two units. So is it your position that this was mere chance or coincidence that they happened to move in the same direction, or could there have been some sort of planning?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness that you referred to, I believe, was Sinan Begovic; and as Ms. Vidovic pointed out yesterday, he didn't see anything, and it was merely hearsay that he -- it was hearsay that formed the basis of what he explained to the Trial Chamber and which led to him drawing the map. So we would say that he is a person who had no real clear knowledge of what went on that day. And, really, what we would draw to your attention is that the evidence shows that there were other groups in the area. Certainly, the Abu Hamza group was based two kilometres away, a very short distance. There was a good road, an asphalt road, that connected the two locations. We would submit that the evidence shows that there is -- it cannot be excluded that it was not one of the other groups that was outside -- in the vicinity at that time. Now, I'd like to turn to the charge of cruel treatment in relation to the Bikosi events. And, here, the Prosecution must prove an intentional act or omission was committed which caused serious mental or physical suffering or injury or constituted a serious attack on human dignity. Your Honours, I'd remind that you on the evidence before the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber, during which that Chamber heard from three witnesses about the Bikosi events, including Berislav Marijanovic and Zdravko Pranjes, two of the same witnesses that we had before us, it held that no reasonable Chamber could conclude that cruel treatment had occurred. It acquitted the accused of that charge, and that was in decision on the motions for acquittal pursuant to Rule 98 bis issued on the 27th of September, 2004. And in our submissions, Your Honours, the evidence in this case as to cruel treatment is not any stronger. The next main claim of the Prosecution is that General Delic had effective control over the Mujahedin on the 8th June 1993. Evidence proves quite clearly that this is not the case. It is for the Prosecution to prove that the perpetrators were at least members of an identifiable group and that General Delic exercised effective control over them at the time the crimes were committed. In our closing brief, at paragraph 253, we have detailed the evidence relating to the timing of the Bikosi killings. A reasonable conclusion would be that it was around noon or early afternoon at the latest. We know that Osman Fusko had already received information about the killings during the afternoon. Therefore, on the evidence, the Prosecution cannot proof that the decision to appoint General Delic as Main Staff commander was taken before the crimes were committed. Even if he had been appointed as Main Staff commander, the applicable standard which must be applied is that he must have exercised effective control over the perpetrators. De facto effective control over his immediate subordinates was not established until after 8.00 p.m. on the 8th June 1993. It follows that his authority could not have been excerpted down further through the chain of command until a later stage. There must be perfect temporal coincidence between the crimes and the effective control, and we submit that there is no way he could have exercised effective control at the time the crimes were committed. Your Honours, I would also note that the Prosecution has not even issued -- hasn't argued the issue of timing in its closing brief at all. Furthermore, in its brief, the Prosecution argues that there are cogent reasons to depart from the majority position in the Hadzihasanovic interlocutory appeal decision. The Prosecution mentions this at paragraph 228 of their brief. However, the Prosecution fails to take into account that this decision has become settled case law. It was specifically endorsed by the Appeals Chamber in the Halilovic Appeals judgement at paragraph 67. No Appeal Chamber judges dissented from that endorsement, and it follows that this is solid jurisprudence that this Chamber is bound to follow. Your Honours, I'll turn to the issue of knowledge concerning Bikosi. Concerning actual knowledge of the Bikosi killings, at paragraph 229 of the Prosecution's brief, it refers to a number of factors which it says that the Chamber can take into account into determining whether actual knowledge of crimes can be inferred. Your Honours, none or few of those factors assist the Prosecution in this case. In fact, if reliance is placed on those factors, they all point to the conclusion that General Delic did not have actual knowledge. The Prosecution claims that General Delic was specifically informed about the 8th of June killings by Witness PW-3. However, the evidence that this led in that regard either lacked reliability or could lead to no reasonable conclusion except that General Delic did not receive any written communications concerning the Bikosi killings or that he was not informed about them in person. As to PW-3's written communications, the Prosecution asserts that the SVK communication centre would have directed Exhibits 170 and 171 to General Delic. In our closing brief, and this is at paragraphs 276 and also 312, we have set out numerous factors which would have led the communications not being forwarded. On Monday, the Prosecution highlighted a number of documents that were sent to General Delic, and this is from a time-period of June to August 1993. And it seems to be the Prosecution's argument that just because you can be sure that General Delic received a handful of communications during that period, you can be certain that he received all communications. Your Honours, it would not be reasonable to make an assumption. For the reasons explained in our closing brief, the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that those documents were ever forwarded to General Delic; and, of course, I'm referring there to Exhibits 170 and 171. Moreover, in its closing brief, at paragraph 238, the Prosecution claims that General Delic failed to respond to the substantive matter contained in Exhibit 174, and that was a letter which warned about the Muslim armed forces threatening to split the 3rd Corps. As we explained in our brief, to the contrary, the evidence shows that General Delic did receive that letter and he reacted by issuing Exhibit 225, and this was something that Witness PW-3 confirmed. So, where does that take us? In our submission, the evidence clearly shows that in those instances where the Trial Chamber can be sure that General Delic received a request for assistance, he reacted and he tried to resolve the problem. The Prosecution's case theory, in a nutshell, is that General Delic received PW-3's communications relating to problems with the Mujahedin; and for reasons unknown, he simply ignored the matter. However, that argument is shown to illogical, when you take into account that on the 16th June 1993, less than one week after the Bikosi killings, and you must bare in mind that General Delic had not been alerted to those killings, he issued Exhibit 163. That exhibit, you will recall, was his order to his subordinate, Hadzihasanovic, to take steps to bring the Gerila Mujahedin group in Zenica within a system of command and control. In that order, General Delic directed that if that could not be carried out, Hadzihasanovic was to, and here I quote the order, "show them no hospitality and eventually disarm them." Your Honours, the evidence, of course, shows that General Delic had no way of enforcing that order because his subordinates actively conspired to undermine it. But the order is important because what it shows was that General Delic was prepared to take steps to try and deal with the Mujahedin groups. Against the background that we have set out in detail in our closing brief, the fact that did he not respond to Exhibits 170 and 171 can only lead the Trial Chamber to the conclusion, the reasonable conclusion, that he did not receive those letters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's the only reasonable conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It can't be excluded, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But is it the only reasonable conclusion? Isn't it also reasonable that he might have just ignored to respond or he may have just forgotten respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, clearly, that is not our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. I understand that is not your position. I'm just saying are there not more than one reasonable conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in due course, you will weigh the evidence and you will take on board our submissions; but, at this stage, we would say that there is no conclusion that he didn't receive those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, as to claim that PW-3 discussed issues with General Delic, and the Prosecution deal with this in paragraph 239 the of their brief, the Trial Chamber attempts to clarify with PW-3 what issues, if any, he discussed led to hopelessly vague and cryptic answers from that witness. No mention is made by PW-3 that he discussed the Mujahedin with General Delic at all. Thus, it was never clarified what issues, if any, were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought he said that when he did discuss with him, he shrugged his shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed, that is it correct, Your Honour. You will see evidence, but what you will see is that immediately after that, he began discussing problems with the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It does seem as if he did discuss with General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, the evidence was that he said he had a discussion with General Delic, but it was not clear what issues were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About the Bikosi issue, and he says General Delic shrugged his shoulders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, our reading of the evidence is that it wasn't clear he was talking about the Bikosi killings, but that is obviously something that the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will check the evidence. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It follows, then, Your Honours, that the Prosecution has failed to prove that General Delic was ever informed of the killings in Bikosi. And on the issue of knowledge, we would want to emphasise that in no way can the Prosecution prove that the perpetrators of the Bikosi killings went on to become members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and this would be crucial for the Prosecution to rely upon the Bikosi killings as being relevant to knowledge that the accused had reason to know that crimes would be later committed by the El Mujahedin Detachment. And my authority for that proposition is the Hadzihasanovic Appeals judgement, at paragraph 30, which makes it clear that the Prosecution must prove that the same group of subordinates were involved in each of the alleged offences. Now, in respect of the results of the investigation that was carried out later on in 1993, the Prosecution goes on to claim in its brief that the result of the October 1993 investigation was indirect contradiction to what General Delic already knew. As I just mentioned, Your Honours, our case is clearly that General Delic did not receive any information about -- prior to President Izetbegovic's letter of the 17th October 1993. On Monday, Your Honour, Judge Moloto stated that, in your recollection, the information that President Izetbegovic reported to General Delic did not conflict with the information from PW-3; and with respect, it is our submission that this is not the case. And, Your Honours, if we could about into private session at this moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So we are still with this issue, Your Honour. What we do know is that following President Izetbegovic's letter, General Delic very properly ordered an investigation. When he received a report of the 3rd Corps, he was entitled to rely upon that. On Monday, the Prosecution claim that the time-period of four days to receive that response was far too little time, but the fact that the report was received quickly should not be held against General Delic. The letter of President Izetbegovic of the 17th October demanded that the report be completed urgently. And the report, of course, came from Dzemal Merdan, who was the second most senior officer within the 3rd Corps, and he was somebody that General Delic would be expected to rely upon and trust. The report also referred to the visit to the burial location by members of the international community and also a prominent Bosnian Croat. It also referred to reports from the 306th Brigade to its superior command. So those references would have bolstered the impression that a proper investigation had been carried out at the lower levels. There was nothing in the report to indicate any unreliability or reason why it could not have been accepted by General Delic, and we would also say that this report, which contained the results of a military security service investigation, would have carried a lot of weight, much more than any unsubstantiated reports of crimes which may have been previously received. Your Honours, on the issue of measures, the Prosecution suggests that the district military prosecutors in Travnik and Zenica never received any criminal reports from the ARBiH concerning the crimes in Bikosi. This is at paragraph 241 of their brief. This has been dealt with in our closing brief, but I would just like to remind you that Exhibit 881 contains a list of selected files taken from the Zenica public prosecutor office. And on page 3 of the B/C/S version of that document, it can be seen that a criminal report was filed against Bezim Spahic, who is the head of Zenica municipality or held a similar function, and that it, inter alia, related to Maline and Bikosi. Also, it can be seen that another criminal report was filed against 3rd Corps commander, Hadzihasanovic. In his testimony, the Zenica public prosecutor, Mr. Hadziselimovic could not exclude the possibility that these criminal reports related to crimes which occurred in Bikosi. Therefore, it follows that the Prosecution has failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that no individual was ever investigated or prosecuted for the Bikosi crimes. Your Honours, at that, I'd like to move to the second main topic, which is the July crime base. As you are aware, the crime base evidence relates to two locations: Livada village and Kamenica camp. Concerning Livada, the Prosecution claims that two captured VRS soldiers, allegedly Predrag Knezevic and Momir Mitrovic, were taken to Livada and killed. First of all, we do not accept that the identities of the two killed men in Livada have been established. The purported identifications by Velibor Trivicevic were made in very difficult circumstances. And, secondly, when regard is had to the exhibits which the Prosecution relies on to establish identity, and these are exhibits 1174 and 644, there is no chain of custody to show that samples from the remains of the bodies found in Bozici village in May 2006 led to the production of DNA reports in October 2006, bearing the names of Knezovic and Mitrovic. Unlike the bodies from the Kamenica grave, no witness came along and explained how samples were taken and sent for analysis. Goran Krcmar's statement doesn't set out what happened, and he doesn't say where the samples were sent to. The identification numbers relating to the bodies do not even properly match the identification numbers on the DNA reports. And, thus, Your Honours, we would say that the Trial Chamber has been left to speculate on the whole process. In this case, the Defence has always made it clear that the forensic evidence was in dispute. It is not stuff for the Prosecution to come along and make two simple references in the footnotes and hope that somehow the Trial Chamber will link them together. This, we would say is not an approach which is appropriate for criminal forum, particularly in a murder case; and, therefore, the Prosecution forensic evidence does not establish beyond a reasonable doubt that the two bodies found were those of Predrag Knezevic and Momir Mitrovic. Secondly, concerning those killings, the most important fact is that there is no way of knowing with certainty who killed the two men and whether they were members of an identifiable group, particularly whether they were members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. You will recall that the evidence was that on hearing noise and shouting, the Mujahedin who was guarding the prisoners ran out of the room and came back carrying a cut-off head. On the Prosecution's theory, it follows that this guard cannot have been the perpetrator. Your Honours, no amount of fancy resolving three dimensional maps can be make the evidence stronger in this case. A criminal trial should not be an exercise in speculation, and the simple fact is that we have no idea who the perpetrators were. We can't tell whether the two men were killed in Livada or elsewhere. It follows the Prosecution cannot prove beyond reasonable doubt that the El Mujahedin members carried out the killing, nor prove that the circumstances of the killing amounted to murder. Moving to the next location, which is within the July crime base, this is Kamenica camp. Concerning Gojko Vujicic, the Prosecution is unable to establish to the criminal standard of proof that the perpetrator of that killing was an El Mujahedin member. Your Honours, it is suggest significant that in its closing brief, at paragraph 253, the Prosecution claims that following the transfer of the prisoners to Kamenica camp, they were visited by non-EMD Bosnian army soldiers. This claim demonstrates that the Prosecution's case theory is that non-EMD personnel had access to the Kamenica camp; and in particular, they had access to the VRS prisoners. I should say that there is no evidence to show who these purported non-EMD persons were. However, at the same time, the Prosecution seems to claim that no one else, apart from the EMD, have access to the camp. You will remember that on Monday, Ms. Sartorio said that there is no evidence in the case that any other group used this camp. We would say that the Prosecution cannot have it both ways. The evidence relating to the camp show that although there were guards manning the entrance to the camp, this was not a high-security arrangement. There was no evidence of any guards manning the parameter of the camp or fencing or barbed wire or anything similar to keep out unwanted visitors. As to the alleged perpetrator of the killing, the witness simply described the perpetrator as a Mujahedin and gave no other description. We don't even know whether that person was a foreigner or a local. And, therefore, on the basis of the Prosecution's position that non-EMD personnel had access to the camp, it is clear that the Prosecution cannot exclude the possibility that the perpetrator was not an EMD member. As to the charge of cruel treatment relating to Kamenica camp in July, the Prosecution claims, at paragraph 252, that the VRS soldiers were subjected to mistreatment from the moment of capture to their last hours in EMD custody. The Prosecution would have you believe that the mistreatment was relentless, it lasted throughout the entire duration of the detention. However, as we set out in the brief, the Prosecution hasn't proved that that was the case. We would invite the Trial Chamber to ask itself whether the prisoners would have left the camp; and, here, I refer to the prisoners -- the witnesses own descriptions about themselves, with only markings to the hands and feet from their binding and a broken tooth but no other injuries. Also, according to Dr. Sikanic, whose Rule 92 bis statement you received, apart from Gojko Vujicic, one of the other prisoners had a serious injury, and that was a person called Goran Stokanovic. In his statement, at page 9, Dr. Sikanic said this man had a big wound on his leg caused by a bullet. However, even though the prisoner was seriously wounded, he obviously survived and was amongst the released prisoners from the camp. And we submit that this does not indicate relentless mistreatment in the camp, but confirms that while they were there, the prisoners received effective medical treatment. As part of its arguments, the Prosecution refers to Velibor Trivicevic's evidence that a boy cut his ears with a knife, this is mentioned at paragraph 290 of their closing brief. And I would remind you that Mr. Trivicevic testified that both ears were still intact and only small cuts made to them. Your Honours, as we explained in our closing brief, in general terms, the conditions for the prisoners improved markedly following that first night in Kamenica camp. And that, Your Honour, brings me to my final topic within the crime base evidence, which is the September crime base. I'll deal, first of all, with the alleged killings with Milenko Stanic and Zivinko Todorovic, which supposedly took place in the vicinity of Kesten. As to Milenko Stanic, the Prosecution relies upon DRW-3 and PW-10. In her evidence, DRW-3 said that she saw the man she referred to as Milenko Stanic being killed by the road leading to Kesten. From her evidence, it was not proven that he laid down his arms and held protected status, and she described how he was killed by automatic rifle fire. However, in contrast, PW-10, a Rule 92 bis witness, stated that he saw Milenko Stanic being killed outside the hall in Kesten. He described how the man left the line in which he was standing and tried to choke a Mujahedin. As a result, the Mujahedin shot him and stabbed him numerous times. And, thus, we would say it is not clear whether DRW-3 and PW-10 are, indeed, talking about the same incident. Furthermore, PW-10's account broadly ties in with what Izet Karahasanovic told the Trial Chamber, and that is he heard that two VRS soldiers had been killed that morning resisting captors, and that led to him recording on his list that two were killed on the road in Kesten. Now, Your Honours, as PW-10 was not called to testify, there was no way for us to query the discrepancies in the evidence there. As to the other alleged victim, Zivinko Todorovic, as we stated in our closing brief, at paragraph 577, when witness DRW-3 was asked whether she knew Zivinko Todorovic, she said no. On Monday, the Prosecution invited to you pay no attention to that answer. They asked you to just simply pay attention to her statement which was given to the Ministry of Interior, in which she described the killing. Your Honours, this is not the way that a criminal Tribunal should work. If a witness is having trouble with recollection, it is always open to a party to seek leave for a document to be shown to a witness for the purpose of them refreshing their memory. There was no such application in this case. Although the witness was testifying by videolink, this still would have been a course of action open to the Prosecution. Your Honours, the Defence position is that there is insufficient evidence to establish that the perpetrators of any killing or killings on the road to Kesten was committed by El Mujahedin members. And that, of course, is one of the questions that you put to us, question number 1. Moving then to the next and most serious allegation that the group of 51 VRS prisoners were murdered. Let me say at the outset that the Prosecution has failed to prove that a group of 51 were seized by members of the EMD and that they were taken to Kamenica camp. Your Honours, we would submit that its case is based on wholly unreliable evidence. Just dealing with the Judge's question number 2 for a moment, if I may, as to how Marko Maric arrived at the Kesten hall. Our submission is that it is unclear whether a person of that name actually arrived at the hall. The only suggestion that he was there was based on the penultimate paragraph of PW-10 statement, where he said that Marko Maric was missing from the group of 52 or 53. But, Your Honours, he didn't say where he last saw the man, he didn't say how you knew the man, or gave any clear information to show that he was there at all. So that's our response to question 2. If we can consider the evidence relating to the seizure of the 51 prisoners there, the initial eye-witness accounts cannot assist the Trial Chamber in determining which group, if any, the Mujahedin belonged to. Yesterday, the Prosecution pointed out -- I should say that on Monday, the Prosecution pointed out that the Rule 92 bis statement of Muhamed Omerasevic, Exhibit 970, was important to prove that the El Mujahedin Detachment took prisoners, and they refer to paragraph 76. However, throughout that statement, the witness refers to the person seizing the prisoners as Arabs. So it is clear that that didn't help establish that they were members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Your Honours, the evidence shows that the EMD members and members of the other Mujahedin groups all dressed in a similar way. They had no set uniforms; they wore combinations of military and civilian dress, sometimes coupled with traditional Arabic clothing; they came from any number of countries; they all wore beards, as did many Bosnian men at that time. The Prosecution relies on documents to show that the EMD were engaged in combat around Kesten on the 10 and 11 September, but the documentary evidence, in fact, shows that the EMD moved away from that area towards Kvrge. Fuad Zilkic confirmed that around the time of the take over on the 11th of September, he saw that EMD advancing towards Kvrge, which explained is about five kilometres away from Kesten. Taken out of context, that may not seem like a particularly long distance; but we would submit that true during an intense military operation in such mountainous and difficult terrain as the Vozuca-Ozren region, that, in fact, is a huge distance. Thus, it cannot be put beyond a reasonable doubt that the group seizing the 51 prisoners from Kesten was one of the several other Mujahedin groups operating in that area. And perhaps most importantly, I remind you that Ali Hamad, who the Prosecution described as one of the most important witnesses in the case, testified that the Abu Zubeir group was present in the Vozuca-Ozren region. And you will recall his map which was carefully drawn by him, and it showed that the Abu Zubeir group moved right through the Kesten area. One thing that the Trial Chamber can be certain of when is that it comes to Mujahedin fighters killing VRS prisoners of war that day, Ali Hamad confirmed that he saw men under the command of Abu Zubeir's deputy carry out a killing. Now, Your Honours, apart from the initial eye-witness accounts, the Prosecution relies on a number of viva voce and Rule 92 bis witness and also some documentry evidence to support its claim. In its opening speech, the Prosecution made it clear that its case is a circumstantial one, and my colleague touched upon this type of evidence yesterday. What I would like to emphasise is that when you come to scrutinize the evidence relating to these crime base witnesses, it is important for the Chamber to look at each witness or each piece of evidence individually to decide whether sufficient reliance can be placed on witness or the evidence. This must be done carefully. If you find that a witness or piece of evidence is sufficiently reliable so that you can plays reliance upon it, then you can move to look at other witness or piece of evidence to see if there is sufficient reliance there. However, what you can't do in order to decide whether the first witness is reliable is, at the same time, look at the second or third witness and say, Well, they're saying the same thing so the first one must be reliable. We say that that would amount to a circular process of corroboration which would be wrong. We've set out at length in our closing brief, the reasons why DRW-3, PW-7, or PW-12 cannot be considered to be reliable witnesses in all respects. Common to all witnesses is the substantial length of time which went by before any of them was asked to prepare a witness statement, coupled with the admission that they all had difficulties in recollection. It is obvious that over time memories can fade, can be lost, or contaminated. And in the case of DRW-3, she made her first statement in November 1999, the same day as DRW-1 and DRW-2. And in the cases of PW-12 and PW-7, they made their first statements in March 2000, although it took PW-12 more than one year to complete his witness statement. And before I move away from the reliability of these witnesses, what I'd like to point out, Your Honours, is that contrary to what the Prosecution stated several times on Monday, at no stage do, we actually challenge the credibility of those three witnesses. We do, of course, challenge their reliability and say that they are mistaken witnesses. Thus, it is our submission that as you scrutinize each witness and each piece of evidence, no hard facts can be drawn. Your Honour, concerning the three women, in our brief, we explained how the evidence shows that they were taken by a different group of persons to those who seized the group of 51 in Kesten. Moreover, the evidence suggests that the women could have been seized by a known group which was not the El Mujahedin Detachment. Contrary to what the Prosecution claimed on Monday, in our brief, we never claimed that DRW-3 only exclusively herd the Bosnian language while she was at that first detention area or location, but what we do say is that was the predominant language spoken. On Monday, the Prosecution also asserted that DRW-3 was told she had been at Kamenica by a military policeman. And what we point out is that that is different to what they claimed in their closing brief, at paragraph 335. There, they suggested that one of the soldiers at the first location identified the place as Kamenica. Your Honours, the reality is that DRW-3's evidence on this point is extremely confusing. At first, she claimed that she was told the name of the initial detention location at the time she left there by a soldier who came in through the door. She then went on to say that when women arrived at school, they were asked whether they knew they had been in Kamenica. She responded, "We did not." Later, she was asked if she had been told the name of the location by the two ARBiH soldiers who had collected them from Podbrezje, and she had made it clear that they, i.e. those two soldiers, had told her that. However, in his testimony, Zakir Alispahic, the policemen who collected the three women, made it clear that he did not inform the women of where they had been, nor did he know where they had been. So, Your Honours, in such circumstances, we submit that it would be unsafe for the Trial Chamber to make any finding that the women or the witness had been told -- that she had been told she was in Kamenica around the time of her intention or subsequent release. In its closing brief, at paragraph 343, the Prosecution alleges the three women were taken from Kamenica to Podbrezje, where they were mentally tortured. The Defence disputes the conditions of treatment at Podbrezje of Vatrostalno amounted to cruel treatment, let alone torture. More importantly, I would, again, remind you that the Prosecution did not plead any alleged mistreatment at the Vatrostalno location as part of its case in either the indictment or the Prosecution pre-trial brief. We first heard about this allegation in the Prosecution closing brief, and it follows, then, that the Defence was not put on notice of any intention that allegations at the Vatrostalno location would form part of the charges. The Trial Chamber should not, therefore, take into account any evidence of alleged mistreatment at Vatrostalno in determining the charges. Your Honours, I will deal with the group of ten prisoners very briefly. In respect of those prisoners, you heard the evidence PW-12 and PW-7. We say that that evidence was contradictory and unreliable, particularly concerning what they were told by others. One of the key pieces of evidence that the Prosecution relies on is PW-12's account that he heard many being taken outside and he heard the sounds of shots. However, if you look at the Prosecution's arguments in its closing brief and the language it uses, it is says he believed detained POWs were brought downstairs. It says PW-12 thinks that those shots were seven soldiers being executed. And we would say, Your Honour, that that language ought to signal an alarm to the Trial Chamber that this is not something that can be relied upon. Your Honour, as to the documents that the Prosecution seek to rely upon, if I can quickly discuss the intercepted fax, exhibit 669, this did not establish at all that the El Mujahedin Detachment took the prisoners. Your Honour, this is was a combat report, you will recall from, the EMD to its superiors abroad, and it boasted that they were in command of the operation. The Prosecution Witness PW-4 testified that the information in the document was not correct. Also, Witness PW-9 was asked about the reference to the Mujahedin taking 60 prisoners. You recall that it was put to him that this didn't refer specifically to the El Mujahedin Detachment, and he replied: "That's right. This could be in reference to any other army unit or, indeed, any other fighters who were involved." And, Your Honour, of course, PW-9 was a witness who was in a position to know the reality of what went on within the El Mujahedin Detachment, and he was adamant that they didn't capture such a large number of prisoners of war. Dealing briefly with the Rule 92 bis evidence the Prosecution relies upon. In PW-10's statement, the Prosecution notes that he describes how ARBiH soldiers saved him from being taken away. They mention in paragraph 328 of their brief. Now, rather than supporting the Prosecution case, the fact that this witness was not offered any information about where his father was or any other prisoners conversely indicates that the ARBiH officers present at the scene did not know who seized the VRS prisoners of war or where they would be taken. The other Rule 92 bis witness that the Prosecution relies on is that of Enes Malicbegovic, where he states that he heard that the EMD had a centre at 13 kilometres and prisoners of war were taken there. However, Your Honours, if regard is had to Mr. Malicbegovic's statement of 18 October 2007, what he, in fact, states is that: "I heard that the EMD had a centre at the 11th or 12th kilometre, and the captured were taken there, but this is only hearsay." He goes on to state that: "Nobody in the military security of the 328 Brigade tried to find out the fate of the captured POWs." Also, in his other statement, dated the 18 January 2006, Mr. Malicbegovic states: "I cannot remember that this Brigade IKM received the information that more than 50 Serb POWs had been taken, and I cannot remember that our service received the report sent by Karahasanovic." Your Honours, rather than call Mr. Malicbegovic as a witness to deal with this issue, the Prosecution instead tendered him as a Rule 92 bis witness. As we set out in our closing brief, the evidence from the other ARBiH witnesses and the EMD witness who came to testify amply shows that there was no evidence to show that the EMD had captured a large group of prisoners. Your Honours, I will quickly deal with the forensic evidence. The Prosecution claims that the remains of seven men exhumed near Kamenica camp were identified. In our closing brief, we have explained the shortcomings in that evidence. While the Prosecution pre-trial brief claims that the remains of only five men were identified from the Kamenica grave, in it's closing brief, the Prosecution claims that a sixth body was found, allegedly Zivinko Todorovic. However, Your Honours, if you look at the evidence relied upon, Exhibit 644 and 655 -- 645, we would say that amongst that evidence, a DNA report cannot be found and, therefore, there is no proof that someone of that name was found there. So, Your Honours, in conclusion, it is our position that the Prosecution has failed to establish that the El Mujahedin Detachment took the group of 51 prisoners and that they were taken and killed at Kamenica camp. Your Honours, I will very briefly deal with the issue of sentencing and say a few words, if I may. Obviously, the need for the Chamber to address itself to this issue is contingent upon a finding of guilt, and our main submission is that General Delic is not guilty. My first point, however, relates to the Prosecution argument, in its closing brief, by the fact that General Delic held the highest military position in the ARBiH, that constituted an aggravating factor. If you look at the Hadzihasanovic Appeals judgement, at paragraph 230, that makes it clear that the position of authority or a position of authority does not in and of itself attract a higher sentence. It is only an abuse of that authority by a superior which could be taken into account. The evidence in this case makes it very apparent that General Delic was not a man who abused his authority. Secondly, Your Honours, and here I will have to take you back to what happened just before the start of this case, where you will recall that the Prosecution attempted to have General Delic's case sent back to Bosnia and Herzegovina. There, it advanced a number of argument which we referred to in our closing brief, and its primary submission was that this case was not sufficiently grave to be tried before this Tribunal. Now, Your Honours, they made that comment at the outset of the case when the Prosecution could look at its case taken at its highest point. Since then, we have had the substantial amount of evidence, and we would say that the Prosecution's case did not improve. In fact, the opposite is true. In its Rule 11 bis motion, the Prosecution stressed that General Delic was different compared to other accused appearing before the Tribunal. And at the Rule 11 bis hearing, Mr. Mundis stressed that there is a quantitative and qualitative difference between a military commander who is ordering crimes and the commander charged under Article 7(3). Your Honours, of course, we would agree with that position. Unlike many of the accused who appear here before this Tribunal, General Delic did not plot or conspire to attack other states. He did not order the legal military activities which brought misery and hardship to innocent persons. Your Honours, the reverse is true. He is a man who from the first moment of taking up his position worked tirelessly to develop and professionalize the Bosnian army, to bring stability to the organisation, to bring uncontrolled groups within the system of command and control. He dealt with rogue units in so far as his authority would permit him. He introduced training for officers in the various branches of the army, and he continuously emphasised the importance of complying with international humanitarian law. Your Honours, the evidence related to summer 1995 and onwards shows that General Delic was heavily engaged in a process to bring peace and stability to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Your Honours, General Delic made a deep contribution to the peace process in that country. It brought stability and it brought the end of a nightmare to many millions of ordinary Bosnians living in that country; and for that, we say that he deserves to be treated with decency and leniency. Your Honours, those are my submissions.
