utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robson. Any rebuttal, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution will have some rebuttal, Your Honours, I would expect perhaps 30 to 45 minutes, if we could, and I would perhaps suggest that we take a recess at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have just a few points to raise in rebuttal. I would like to start, however, by indicating a correction that was pointed out by the Defence in Madam Vidovic's closing yesterday of footnote 350 in the Prosecution's final trial brief should actually be corrected. The footnote refers to Exhibit 65. That should read Exhibit 97. And perhaps, once again, I put together some PowerPoint slides. That's clearly indicated. If you take a look, Your Honours, at table 4 in the Prosecution's final trial brief, and compare that to the entries in Exhibit 97, which again is what the footnote 350 should be, we would submit that clearly the names indicated on table 4 are reflected, in fact, in Exhibit 97 in this slide, we would submit, demonstrates that point quite clearly. But, again, footnote 350 in the Prosecution's final trial brief should read Exhibit 97, rather than Exhibit 65. While on this point, an issue was raised by my learned colleague Mr. Robson this morning concerning the perpetrators or alleged perpetrators of the crime in Bikosi. And I draw the Trial Chamber's attention to a comparison of Exhibit 65 and Exhibit 97. What we have down here is pulled up names that are listed on Exhibit 65, a list of transferred soldiers to the El Mujahedin Detachment. Those names which we've highlighted are names which also appear on Exhibit 97, which, Your Honours will recall, is an exhibit from February 1996, listing the personnel within the El Mujahedin Detachment. And I raise this in the contest of comments made by Mr. Robson this morning because with respect to entry number one, Ishak Aganovic, and entry number 38, Zihmad Sejdic, Your Honours will recall those two names were mentioned by the survivors of the Bikosi incident as being among the group of people who came out of the Poljanice camp and were responsible for the crimes in Bikosi. And we would submit, if a quick search of the transcripts for those two name, number one, Ishak Aganovic, and number 2, Zihmad Sejdic, number 38 on the list, would clearly lead you to evidence that would point to not only the alleged perpetrators of the event in Bikosi, but also the fact that those two individuals were members of the El Mujahedin Detachment as late as the end of the war. That is reflected on Exhibit 97 listing EMD personnel in that detachment. Let me turn now to the next topic that we would like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention to. Both Madam Vidovic yesterday and Mr. Robson earlier today touched upon the issue of faxes sent abroad by the El Mujahedin Detachment. And at this point in time, we would simply like to draw the Trial Chamber's attention both to what was said yesterday, on pages 23 and 43, with respect to faxes being sent to Milan, but also to put fort the Prosecution position with respect to any such faxes or intercepted communications going from the El Mujahedin Detachment to sources outside of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Prosecution argues, Your Honours, that these faxes were primarily propaganda tools which were designed to attract funding for the El Mujahedin Detachment. And as a result, we would submit that they do not possess the value to which the Defence would attach to them and has urged the Trial Chamber to attach to them. We based that upon the testimony of some of the witnesses who have appeared before Your Honours. For example, PW-9 testifying on 17 April was asked: "We've seen today documents produced by the press centre in terms of public relations aspect to be send abroad." And he answered: "Yes, one could put it that way. He went on, in respect to the bulletin that he was questioned about that indicated a call to Jihad, to say: "The recipients of the reports from the detachment passed the information on and conducted some sort of propaganda as it were for the detachment. He went on to say: "Let me give you an illustration which will give you a clear idea of how this worked. In Saudi Arabia, there was Abu Muaz who was in charge of raising founds and who received the reports from the El Mujahedin Detachment. He used that information to visit Sheiks and rich men, potential donors. He also brought along the video recordings that we made in the detachment. It was also distributed, and as a result of that, donations and funds flowed in. We would submit, Your Honours, the fact that the El Mujahedin Detachment sought support from abroad does not in any way impact upon the control which the ARBiH exerted over that unit, because the purpose of those reports in the sense of receiving funds from abroad and/or perhaps encouraging other men to joined El Mujahedin Detachment and to enter Bosnia from abroad were consistent with the war efforts directed by the ARBiH. These reports were sent both to raise money and for propaganda purposes. That is the proper emphasise that we would submit needs to be attached to these documents. Again, the testimony of PW-9 on this point is particularly important: "These funds that were being received from outside, what was being done with this money or these funds?" He answered: "The funds were used for purchasing ammunition, weapons, food, clothes, equipment, whatever the El Mujahedin Detachment needed, communications devices, vehicles, and so on." "Question: All of these items that you have listed were being used in order to advance the war aims?" "Answer: Largely, to a great extent. For the most part, the purpose was to advance the war aims." If I could just briefly go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: There was other evidence that Your Honours heard, however, on the army directing the EMD's war efforts. Mr. Awad testified about this. He was asked: "Who set the combat priorities for the detachment?" He answered: "It is logical that the priorities would be set by the commanders, either of the corps or the operations group; that is, the persons who had several units under their command, because the El Mujahedin Detachment as a small units cannot determine where others would attack, nor where they themselves would attack. So it is only logical and normal for the people who are in charge of several brigades or several units to plan and to determine the priorities ..." Let's turn to Exhibit 1394. The Defence have argued, and in referring to Exhibit 1394, as indicating that the EMD turned down a number of operations. The Prosecution would respectfully submit that in this aspect, Exhibit 1394 is unreliable because the evidence has shown that during the existence of the El Mujahedin Detachment, particularly with respect to 1994 and 1995, that unit failed to carry out combat on two occasions, in the summer of 1994 and in November of 1994. Again, Aiman Awad was asked about this and testified that there was only one refusal to carry out an attack which occurred in November 1994, and you see the reference to that on the screen. The Prosecution, Your Honours, submits that the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina could and did rely on the El Mujahedin Detachment. Yesterday, Madam Vidovic argued that the army couldn't count on the EMD. We submit, with all due respect, that that's not correct. The most important assignments in military operations during the relevant time-period and which are the focus of this case were given to the El Mujahedin Detachment. And we would submit that this demonstrates more clearly than anything else that the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina could and did rely upon the El Mujahedin Detachment. Again, Ali Hamad was asked a question by Judge Harhoff: "How closely were the details arranged between you and the ABiH forces on the technical level?" Ali Hamad: "Us foreign fighters would always be in the first strike. They would mostly ask us for help when they felt that they could not liberate an area or an elevation by themselves." One particularly striking element or attack that fits squarely into this category were the operations concerning Paljenik which was, as Your Honours will recall from the evidence and the site visit, an extremely important feature in the overall campaign to liberate the Vozuca pocket. And it was the El Mujahedin Detachment that was given that task, a task which they successfully met. The value and reliability of the El Mujahedin Detachment was clearly proved by the time Operations Proljece 2 and Farz were executed in July and September 1995. With respect to Proljece 2, Exhibit 606 makes it clear that the El Mujahedin Detachment is the primary leader in the upcoming task. As I've indicated, and as the Chamber is obviously well aware, a number of witnesses, including Mr. Hajderhodzic, Mr. Jusic, and Mr. Ribo all testified about the importance of the Paljenik feature in the overall campaign that was taken and undertaken in 1995. Let me turn now to the issue of the late-President Izetbegovic and the El Mujahedin Detachment. Yesterday, Madam Vidovic made several references that would seem to point to President Izetbegovic and his direct relationship or control over the El Mujahedin Detachment, and you can see those references on the screen in front of you. We would submit that President Izetbegovic's decisions concerning the army and its constituent units, including the El Mujahedin Detachment, were informed by General Delic. You will recall the Defence expert Mr. Cornish who was asked about this. And he testified that: "If civil leadership is making decisions about the use of armed forces, then it is fundamental and at least common sense for that decision making to be informed by military expertise." This is particular important, we would submit, in situations such as the one that was present or the situation as it existed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war, when the extended War Presidency included General Delic among its membership. We would submit that true there is evidence before the Trial Chamber that President Izetbegovic trusted General Delic. We have the 92 ter statement of Mr. Buljubasic to that effect. The Presidency appointed him. He was the most influential person in the presidency supporting Delic; that is, Mr. Izetbegovic. As I've indicated, and as described more clearly in paragraph 50 of our final trial brief, General Delic was a member of the expanded Presidency along with, obviously, President Izetbegovic. Mr. Jusic testified about this as well. He was asked: "Apart from the formal Presidency sessions, were there other meetings that you were aware of that took place where members of the Presidency -- which included members of the Presidency?" "Yes, there were, and it wasn't just that I was aware of them; everyone knew about them. These were meetings attended by certain members of the Presidency, the president and usually the man in charge of the army. Earlier it was Halilovic and later Delic." We also know from evidence Your Honours have heard that when Alija Izetbegovic visited army units, General Delic accompanied him. There's also evidence from General Divjak that General Delic communicated with President Izetbegovic on a regular basis, "probably daily," testified General Divjak. The Prosecution submits that the evidence supports the notion that General Delic maintained indirect control over the El Mujahedin Detachment through his authority over the 3rd Corps commander, and that this control extended throughout the indictment period. Yesterday, Madam Vidovic made some claims or argued that the BiH army had effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment, not General Delic. We would submit that nothing in the evidence suggests that General Delic did not exert command authority over the 3rd Corps commander; and, of course, at the relevant time-periods in the indictment, the El Mujahedin Detachment was a constituent unit of the 3rd Corps. Again, Mr. Buljubasic testified that: "Relations between General Delic and the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Mahmuljin, were respectful and professional. They were the same as relations between the general and any other corps commander or any other subordinate commander ..." The Defence have also argued, with respect to EMD compliance with ARBiH orders, that the El Mujahedin Shura meat ultimate decisions concerning the detachment. We would submit that it was irrelevant that there was discussion about combat orders or the disbandment of the EMD within the Shura; rather, it is sufficient that the orders issued by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were complied with by the El Mujahedin Detachment. We would also submit, based upon the evidence of General Sead Delic, that the Shura itself, the concept of the Shura, was not uncommon in other ARBiH units. He testified that General Brzina assisted him in establishing the 9th Muslim Brigade because there were references in that unit to a Shura, and General Sead Delic testified that did he not know what the Shura was. The Defence also are as part of the Defence theory concerning the Islam Cultural Centre argued that Sheik Anwar Saban was the de facto authority over the El Mujahedin Detachment, and this was the argument put forth by Madam Vidovic yesterday. The Prosecution submits that there is no evidence that demonstrates that Saban disrupted General Delic's effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment; rather, the detachment complied with instructions from the ARBiH. What do we base this on? Again, the evidence. There was reference yesterday by Madam Vidovic to the issuance of a fatwa. Well, PW-9 testified about that. And the evidence on this issuance of a fatwa by Mr. Saban concerned a single incident relating to elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is evidence that Saban complied with the orders issued by General Delic. In relation to the disbandment of the EMD, Exhibit 365 reports that: "He pointed out at the end they would accept all decisions of our political and military leadership." Your Honours, this is my last opportunity to address you in these proceedings, and it has been truly a privilege and honour to lead the Prosecution team in this case, but also to work with all of the professionals on Madam Vidovic's team, as well as the hard-working members of the Chamber's staff and the registry. Cases are rarely, if ever, lost as a result of the eloquence of closing arguments, and this case is no different from most in that respect. The Trial Chamber in this case has heard the evidence, it has fully engaged the witnesses and the parties throughout the case, and as the Trial Chamber retires to deliberate and reach the important findings which it has the obligation and responsibility to make, the Prosecution has no doubt that the Chamber will reach the correct conclusions. Let me close, if I might, by commenting upon just a few of the final arguments put to you earlier this morning by Mr. Robson. Mr. Robson told you that General Delic was, and I'm quoting now, "a man who from the first moment of taking up his position worked tirelessly to professionalize the Bosnian army, to bring controlled groups within the system of command and control. He dealt with rogue units in so far as his authority would permit." The Prosecution would ask that in considering this argument, that you ask yourselves whether the actions of the accused in forming the El Mujahedin Detachment are consistent with the notion of professionalizing the Bosnian army. We would ask you, with all due respect, to consider whether General Delic, in this case, used the full strength of his authority to deal with rogue units. Mr. Robson continued. He said this morning: "Your Honours, the evidence relating to summer 1995 and onwards shows that General Delic was heavily engaged in a process to bring peace and stability to Bosnia and Herzegovina. General Delic made a deep contribution to the peace process in that country. It brought stability and it brought the end of a nightmare to many millions of ordinary Bosnians." Again, we would ask the Trial Chamber to consider whether the honours and awards bestowed upon the El Mujahedin Detachment by General Delic's army are consistent with these arguments. Was his appearance and his comments at farewell ceremony for the El Mujahedin Detachment consistent with the off-stated goals of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for a multi-ethnic army. The Prosecution urges the Trial Chamber to reach the only reasonable conclusions based upon the totality of the evidence in this case. The accused exercised effectively control over the Mujahedin from Poljanice and then the El Mujahedin Detachment, a unit which he formed, throughout the indictment period. He failed to prevent crimes from happening, he failed to punish the perpetrators after being known or being put on notice that crimes had occurred. The accused is guilty of the charges set forth in the indictment; and as a result both of the crimes and the position held by the accused throughout the indictment period, the Prosecution urges a sentence of 15 years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mundis. Any rejoinder, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, definitely, and thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start with some of the last observations Mr. Mundis made, related to the acts of the accused regarding the El Mujahedin Detachment. The Prosecution has just told us, and this is what it has been saying right from the start, that General Delic is the one who formed the El Mujahedin Detachment. Your Honours, let me remind you, once again, about what we can see from the evidence. Your Honours, we have two situations here that operated when the El Mujahedin Detachment was established. The first element is -- the first situation existed in the BH army and among the international community that was trying hard to settle the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In controvertible evidence that you heard from witness PW-3 and from General Divjak indicated that the international community insisted that the Mujahedin should be put under control. The international community insisted that -- on that in its contacts with President Izetbegovic. You heard about that. And it is beyond a reasonable doubt in light of those two testimonies of those two Prosecution witnesses that the decision to set up this detachment was made elsewhere. It was a political decision, and General Delic did not have any authority over it. It was a decision made by his superior who had cumulative powers. President Izetbegovic not only had powers as the president of the Presidency, he also had powers as the head of the Supreme Command, somebody who headed the Supreme Command of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Not only that, President Izetbegovic had explicit powers envisaged in Article 10 on the Decree on the Armed Forces - that's Exhibit 22 - to represent the armed forces in context with both internal and external elements. So the decision to set up the detachment, or, rather, the order to set up the detachment, is merely an order that General Delic relayed further, and it stemmed from a decision made by his superior. Your Honours, we devoted a large part of our brief to the requirements that a decision of an accused must meet in order to be relevant and taken into account in the context of his alleged effective control. And now I want to go back to what is the -- what is actually at issue in this trial. Your Honours, you don't have in the dock the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or General Mahmuljin, the commander of the 3rd Corps. You have in front of you General Delic who was the commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And the question of all questions in this case is whether General Delic had effective control, exercised effective control, not whether General Mahmuljin had effective control or whether BH army had or exercised effective control. And while I'm on this issue, let me say one more thing, God forbid should the Defence accept that at any point that the BH army actually exercised effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment. This is -- this did not really come out that way in what I was saying, so I want to stress that. But let me now go back to the issuing of effective control as the key issue here. Today, the Prosecutor tried to say that I was trying to prove that President Izetbegovic had control over the detachment. Your Honours, the gist of my comments yesterday was something else. I said that the Prosecution, itself, talking about the responsibility of General Delic, in paragraph 161, said that the El Mujahedin actually negotiated with President Izetbegovic and then General Mahmuljin actually carried out those orders. Your Honours, the issue of effective control involves the following elements: General Delic issues an order, and this order has to stem from his own authority, and then his subordinates obey the commander of the 3rd Corps, the commander of the 35th Division, and finally Abu Maali as the commander of the El Mujahedin Detachment, and all the way down to the actual persons who carried this order out. This is very far removed from reality in this case. The Prosecution drew your attention to this fact in the brief, when they mention President Izetbegovic and say that he negotiated and arranged things with the El Mujahedin Detachment and then some commander actually carried out this out. Your Honours, this goes outside of the chain of command. This is not part of the chain of command. Yesterday, the Prosecution mentioned several times meetings at different levels. They should serve as a marker of the existence of effective control. Your Honours, effective control means that things are done within the chain of command; nothing more and nothing less. The moment the detachment commander, Abu Maali, if he really was subordinated to the 35th Division, sidesteps the commander of the division and arranges anything with the corps commander, at that point the chain of command is in pieces and there is no control. Your Honours, be that as it may, I would just like to remind you of something that is very important when we're talking about effective control. Effective control is clearly delineated in the jurisprudence, for instance, in the Blaskic case that we ask not really touch upon all that much. In that case, it has been made quite clear, evidence must support or must show that the perpetrators are those who obey the orders of the accused in question, not the orders of any other command. At the point when it is established that there is a parallel chain of command, there is no effective control anymore. Your Honours, I say now that, in this case, it is not that the Defence actually created this reasonable doubt about there being effective control. We went one step beyond. The Defence has, in fact, managed to prove that there existed a parallel chain of command and the parallel chain of reporting. Let me now go back to the documents that the Prosecution talked about today, in order to tell you that you should not give much weight to the documents in Milan. Your Honour, as regards those documents from Milan that were found in the institute in Milan, in Sheik Anwar Saban's office, I would like to classify them in two categories. One category is the one that the -- my learned friend Mr. Mundis talked about. These are the bulletins originating from the El Mujahedin Detachment. But, Your Honours, there is another category of documents that is very important for this case. We're not talking about only bulletins from the El Mujahedin Detachment. You saw in front of you military reports, pure and simple, that had nothing to do with what witness PW [as interpreted] was talking about. This PW-9 actually confirmed the accuracy of those reports. He confirmed that those were military reports. So we have bulletins, but we also have military reports. Could we now please look at Exhibit 1201, page 3, of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I the only one hearing noises?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have D001-1238. That is the page in the Bosnian. That's for the accused to be able to follow, D001-1238. Your Honours, this is what I'm talking about. What you see here is a fax to the Islam Cultural Centre in Milan. Look at this, Your Honours. This is a report. This is a report on the battle at Kajin Sopot. We have heard a lot about this. This is a detailed military report about all of the aspects of the battle. Can we please go to the next page. Your Honours, this is no appeal to collect aid for the El Mujahedin Detachment; this is a military report, pure and simple. Could we please turn the page in the English. We would like to see the signature. That's the next page. Your Honours, the report that we have just seen, E-1201, is a military report being submitted by the leader of the battalion, Abu El-Maali, to Sheik Saban in the Islamic Cultural Centre. He is not asking for anything at all; he is just reporting on the battle. The next exhibit, 1389. This is the Proljece battle, Pocilovo [phoen]. It's a pure military report. It is nothing more than that, and it describes in detail the battle that took place. It starts with the weather and concludes with the number of those killed in battle. I'm sure you will remember - I'm not sure we have time to track this down - but you remember the report on the dead and wounded, all the reports being submitted to the Sheik Saban. Therefore, it is simply not true, as the OTP would have you believe, that the detachment was sending these reports in order to obtain materiel assistance. That is a far cry from the actual truth. Can we now please look at Exhibit 1390. This will help us understand the role played by the Sheik Saban, 1390. Before we see the exhibit come up on our screens, please allow plea to remind you that the issue of appointing commanders to the unit and within the unit is a key issue in terms of effective control. If the BH army at any of its levels is simply unable to appoint those commanders, if it is the Sheik who is appointing these commanders and dispatching them from somewhere abroad, then, Your Honours, there can be no talk of any sort of control at all. These are not appeals for assistance. What this is is commanders being dispatched to Bosnia. We're talking about page 3 in the English. Your Honours, this is a another document from the Milan-based institute. This is an intercept of a phone conversation between Anwar Saban and Abdul Aziz, another person that we've heard a lot about throughout these proceedings. This document tells that the Sheik, Saban, is dispatching commanders to Bosnia. Look at this, the first sentence. Abdul Aziz: "Tell me, are there any lads over there leaving for Bosnia?" And then Anwar Saban replies: "I'm the one organizing their departure. It is working well. I'm also deal with another matter. If it works out, we'll be able to dispatch many people." And then again: "Abu el-Haris," who you remember is one of the commanders of the El Mujahid Detachment, "Abu el-Haris has called me from Bosnia telling me that he needed several commanders along various front lines." It is obvious that the Sheik Saban is the one who makes decisions regarding commanders. You will also remember Document 1394. This is a document that the OTP referred to a moment ago. There is no doubt that in this document, the detachment is trying to justify itself by explaining that they are not under the control of the army. Even if we disregard this aspect for the moment, this is crucial evidence, needless to say; but, even so, just look at the other portions of this document. It should be easy enough for you, Your Honours, to understand that the El Mujahedin Detachment, whenever there is an issue that arises whenever any of the aspect of its activity is at stake, they go to the Sheik. They go to Saban, and they justify themselves and explain themselves to him for the manner in which they work: We don't need any rules or regulations for this. We don't need any laws. When are justifications offered? Who are these justifications ordered to? To one superior, and not just some imaginary person. Your Honours, the Defence team has here pointed out the existence not just of reasonable doubt. It is beyond reasonable doubt that we have succeeded in proving this. We took the burden of proof upon yourselves. We shouldered the burden of proof. Why? The OTP had been sitting on all this evidence for years. They didn't dare accuse General Delic, and they wouldn't if they knew there was such evidence that existed. They left us in a situation where we had no choice but to shoulder the burden of proof, which have done successfully to the very end, if I may say. The OTP have simply failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that General Delic in any way, directly or indirectly, controlled this unit. As to the OTP's allegation that Delic was indirectly in control of the El Mujahedin Detachment, well, let me tell you this. Firstly, throughout this trial, the OTP have been behaving as though there was no indictment, to start with. Firstly, they accused General Delic of ordering Proljece 2 operation in July. Secondly, of ordering Operation Farz. Thirdly, of having been in command of those operations. And, fourthly, of making use of the El Mujahedin Detachment for those operations. Your Honours, quite simply, none of this is true. General Delic never ordered those operations. General Delic was never in command of those operations. If you look at the theories that the OTP have been offering for two days now, General Delic is suddenly informed that the lines have shifted. But this is very far from being in command. It is a far cry for being in effective control. Your Honours, the OTP must establish some sort of a nexus between the accused, on the one hand, and the developments that actually occurred and that he stands indicted for. There is no nexus, and we need to talk about the developments described in the indictment, not something else. Based on what Mr. Mundis, my learned friend, told you a while ago, Rasim Delic might as well be responsible for anything at all that happened within the area of responsibility of any of the BH army's units. Yes, he was at the head of the General Staff. Yes, the General Staff was a body - in terms of regulations, I mean - that was in charge of the corps commanders. But international humanitarian law makes him in no way responsible, and the requirement is proof that he had effective control, and they just failed to prove that, and they certainly didn't prove that he exercised effective control through the 3rd Corps commander. No. When all of this was going on, was it conceivable that he was in some sort of a chain of command to do with the El Mujahedin Detachment? If so, he would certainly have been resubordinated to the commander of the 35th Division as the very least. That would have been the situation de jure, resubordinated to the 35th Division. The situation being what it was General Mahmuljin had nothing whatsoever to do with that. The 3rd Corps had been resubordinated. Fine. General Delic's first subordinate would not have -- even he would not have been the one to be in effective control or to effectively report to General Delic on what was going on. Your Honours, I'm wrapping up. I'm going to talk about the reports. This is an essential aspect of effective control. Reports on this unit, on those developments, should have reached General Delic. They ought to have reached General Delic in terms of him being informed about the activities of that unit, and especially being informed about the fact that that unit was involved in this or involved in that. Your Honours, we have gone through mountains of documents, the summaries, the reports, making perfectly clear that any combat reports were being sent to Kajin -- Kakanj, the Kakanj command post. They would be summed up there and then summaries forwarded to Sarajevo to General Delic. Two or three words; no more, really. Your Honours, not only was the situation like this. According to international humanitarian law, you are responsible for reviewing the situation that the accused was facing at the time. Look at what was going on in July. You saw the evidence, didn't you? Not only did he receive nothing at all from the El Mujahedin Detachment, not only did nothing ever reach Sarajevo. Even if it had, Your Honours, Rasim Delic, the man, the general, at the time, was at a conference in Croatia, in Split, Croatia. That has been proven by documents beyond reasonable doubt. After that, this man was in command of the Sarajevo operation. He was extremely busy with this situation that he to deal with, the dreadful situation in Sarajevo. You saw the video-clip yesterday, Your Honours, the video showing the Sarajevo victims. That was what General Rasim Delic was trying to deal with. He was trying to the blockade lifted so that hundreds of thousands of Sarajevo's inhabitants might live. That was the struggle that he was facing. Just think about it for a while, Your Honours. Is it realistic to imagine Rasim Delic keeping track of thousands of small factions and groups and units facing the situation that he was facing. He was simply unable to receive any sort of information like that in July, nothing at all about the El Mujahedin Detachment, let alone, Your Honours, how ludicrous is it to claim that General Delic would have been in the situation at the Kuala Lumpur conference to be on the receiving end of information from Bosnia and exercise any sort of control over what was going on thousands and thousands of miles away in Bosnia. This is entirely ludicrous. It is entirely inconceivable. There is the time-gap, after all. And then I know the Chamber understands that the assistance being shipped into Bosnia by Islamic countries was a crucial matter for the Bosniaks' survival. This is no longer a matter of the BH army. This is no longer a matter of the BH army command. This was a matter of survival. This was a matter of ensuring the survival of hundreds and thousands of Muslims who were there, Muslims and others who had, up to this point in time, been killed, persecuted, raped, and so on and so forth. Try to understand: This is what Delic was busy doing at the time. He was trying to come up with aid. He was trying to come up with some help from the international community to have the blockade lifted from these unfortunate towns and cities that were under siege. You need to keep in mind the situation that the accused was facing at the time, the accused himself. That is what international justice expects from you. There is another thing that is very important as far as Operation Farz is concerned, Your Honours, and we have proven this beyond reasonable doubt. He was being represented by General Hadzihasanovic at the time. We have also proven that any reports to do with Operation Farz -- that no reports to do with Operation Farz were ever sent to General Delic. They were being sent to President Izetbegovic directly and no one else. These are the facts of this case. These are the facts. Again, Your Honours, we move that Rasim Delic be acquitted on all counts of the indictment. Last but not least, we would like to thank the Chamber, for its patience, understanding, and cooperation. Likewise, our heart-felt thank you goes to our learned friends from the OTP. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic. Any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That brings us to the conclusion of the closing arguments. The Chamber will now retire for deliberations and in due course will convene the Court for purposes of delivery of judgement. Court stands adjourned sine die. Cour adjourned.
